messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Worker
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 52

**Patient Vignette: "David"**

David is a 53-year-old married man, a social worker by profession, who presents for therapy at the urging of his wife. He is a tall, lean man with a weary stoop to his shoulders, and he speaks in a careful, measured tone, as if he is constantly editing his own words. He is a man who has spent his career listening to the worst stories people have to tell, believing he could absorb their pain and help them carry it. Now, he is finding that he cannot carry his own.

The event that changed everything happened eight months ago. David was leaving a community center late on a Tuesday evening, after a particularly difficult group session with veterans. The parking lot was quiet, and he was thinking about a client’s disclosure, his mind still in the room with the group. He did not hear the footsteps until a hand clamped over his mouth from behind. He was forced into the back of his own car, a man he did not know, who smelled of sweat and cheap beer. David did not fight. He is a man who has been trained in de-escalation, in the art of non-resistance to prevent harm. He tells me, with a hollow laugh, that he “did everything right.” He used the techniques he teaches to victims: he stayed calm, he spoke in a low voice, he did not make eye contact. He complied. He was raped in the back seat of his own sedan, and then the man drove him to a remote industrial park and left him there, naked from the waist down, shivering in the dark.

David did not call the police. He drove himself home, took a shower so hot it left his skin red and raw, and told his wife he had been in a minor car accident. He went to work the next day. For three months, he did not tell a soul. He says he was “processing it.” But what he was really doing was trying to erase it.

The symptoms crept in like a slow leak. At work, he began to avoid certain clients—specifically, men with certain body types or voices that reminded him of the attacker. He found himself excusing himself from sessions early, his heart hammering. He started locking his office door, a thing he had never done in twenty years. He could no longer sit with his back to the room. His colleagues noticed he was “off,” but he blamed it on burnout.

At home, the intimacy with his wife became impossible. He flinched when she touched his shoulder. He began sleeping on the couch, telling her he was having trouble with his back. He stopped driving his own car, claiming it needed repairs, and took her minivan instead. The smell of his own vehicle—the faint scent of his own coffee and the leather seats—made his throat close up. He has not driven at night in four months.

The worst part, he says, is the shame. Not the shame of the assault itself, but the shame of how he responded. He is a social worker. He is supposed to be the protector, the one who knows what to do. He tells me, with a tremor in his voice, that he is haunted by the thought that he “let it happen.” He should have fought. He should have screamed. He did what he taught others to do, and he cannot forgive himself for it.

Last week, he was walking through the grocery store and a man in a blue jacket brushed past him. David dropped his basket, his vision went white, and he found himself crouched on the floor between the canned goods, his hands over his head, waiting for something that was not coming. He stayed there for ten minutes. A store employee asked if he needed medical help. He said he was fine, stood up, and walked out, leaving his cart full of groceries behind.

He came to see me because his wife told him she was afraid. She said he was “not there anymore.” He agrees. He feels like a ghost in his own life. He can still do his job, but only by compartmentalizing with a ferocity that exhausts him. He can still laugh with his children, but the laugh sounds borrowed. He is a man who spent his life helping others hold their stories, and now he cannot bear to hold his own.
